home.eyebrow: A free, open-source school of mathematics
home.title: Mathematics, from counting to categories — for everyone, everywhere.
home.lead: The Lumenary is a growing curriculum where every idea is explored three ways: understood by people, proved precisely, and tested by computation. Learn at your own pace. No accounts, no ads, no streaks.
home.modesTitle: Three ways of knowing, woven together
home.modesLead: Each concept is taught through three complementary modes that reinforce one another rather than living in separate books.
home.modeHText: Intuition, examples, pictures, conjectures and clear human proofs. Not just how — but why it’s true.
home.modeFText: Precise definitions and machine-checked proofs in Lean 4. Assumptions made explicit; nothing claimed that didn’t compile.
home.modeCText: Python experiments you can run in your browser. Learn the difference between evidence, approximation and proof.
home.sequenceLead: Five connected lessons, from sorting a basket of fruit to composing functions — the doorway to category theory.
home.trailsLead: Optional side-paths for the curious. They never count against you, and they always lead back to where you were.
home.entryLead: Every learner begins somewhere. Pick the door that fits — you can always wander.
home.principleQuote: Master the present. Glimpse the future. Never require the future to understand the present.
home.honestLead: The Lumenary is at the very beginning. Here is exactly what has been built and checked so far.
home.notYetReviewed: No content has yet been reviewed by a human mathematician or educator. That review is the next essential step.
home.valuesLead: Truthfulness, humility, generosity and wonder shape how The Lumenary is built — and every learner is welcome, whatever they believe.

lab.title: Math laboratory
lab.lead: Experiment, calculate, simulate — and learn what a computation can and cannot tell you. Every experiment runs in your browser and is also tested automatically.
lab.scratchLead: A blank Python sandbox with SymPy and NumPy available.
lab.ladderLead: Computers are wonderful at producing evidence. Proof is a different thing. Here is how the kinds of computational evidence differ.

ladder.exact: Arithmetic on integers or fractions with no rounding. The answer is exactly right — for the inputs computed.
ladder.symbolic: Algebra on symbols, like expanding (x + 1)². As trustworthy as the rules the software was built on.
ladder.exhaustive-finite: Checking every case of a finite problem. A genuine proof — but only for that finite set of cases.
ladder.counterexample: One case where a general claim fails. A single counterexample really does disprove a “for all” statement.
ladder.numerical: Floating-point approximations. Fast and useful, but rounding errors can creep in and must be understood.
ladder.experimental: Trying many examples. Builds confidence and suggests conjectures, but cannot prove a statement about infinitely many cases.
ladder.statistical: Estimates from random samples, with uncertainty. Tells us what is likely, never what is certain.
ladder.proof: A logical argument that covers every case. Human proofs explain why; Lean proofs are checked by a machine.

formal.title: Formal mathematics laboratory
formal.lead: Lean 4 is a programming language and proof assistant: a computer checks every step of a proof. Here you can read every formal proof used by The Lumenary — and the exact report of what compiled.
formal.whatIsText: A declaration is labelled formally verified only if it appears in the latest Lean build report, compiled without errors, and does not depend on sorry. We also list which axioms each proof relies on.
formal.scope: Current scope: core Lean 4 only. Mathlib integration is planned; Mathlib analogues are named but have not been checked against Mathlib.
formal.exercisesLead: Each exercise contains a sorry for you to replace. Open it in the Lean web editor, or clone the repository and run lake build.

practice.title: Practice
practice.lead: Exercises with hints and explanations. Take as many tries as you like — there are no scores, timers or streaks.

languages.title: Languages
languages.lead: The Lumenary aims to teach in every language people learn mathematics in. This registry is honest about where things stand: right now, six demonstration languages have interface translations, and only English is the canonical source.
languages.countriesLead: Every UN member state has a target language in the registry. Where a country has no legally designated official language, we record that fact rather than inventing one.
languages.numeralsLead: Numbers are formatted with each locale’s conventions, and mathematics stays left-to-right inside right-to-left text.

verification.title: Verification
verification.lead: The Lumenary aims to be more trustworthy than ordinary AI-generated material. This page reports exactly what has been checked, by what, and what has not.
verification.humanText: No lesson, translation or exercise has yet been reviewed by a qualified human mathematician, educator or translator. Agreement among AI systems is not treated as evidence of correctness.
verification.leanSummary: {n} declarations compiled with {toolchain}; {sorry} depend on sorry. {library} apply a library theorem, {independent} are proved here, {definition} are definitions.
verification.computeSummary: {passed} of {total} experiments ran and passed their tests. pytest: {tests} passed, {failed} failed.
verification.contentSummary: {passed} automated checks passed, {failed} failed (schemas, prerequisite graph, registries, translations, answer parsing).

limitationsList.l1: Only five lessons and seven Wonder Trails exist; every other topic is planned.
limitationsList.l2: Lean proofs use core Lean 4 only; Mathlib integration is planned.
limitationsList.l3: The Pyodide (browser) runtime and the CPython test runtime are different Python versions; the experiments were checked to print identical output, but that check is not yet automated.
limitationsList.l4: No accessibility audit has been carried out.
limitationsList.l5: The language and country registries contain entries flagged for review.

narrators.margaretQ: What happens if we calculate it?

sort.title: The market sorting game
sort.subtitle: Pick something from the basket, then pick the box it belongs in.
sort.empty: The basket is empty — everything has been sorted!
sort.nowPick: Now choose a box for the {item}.
sort.lookAgain: Look again at the {item}. Which box does it belong in?
sort.successColour: Wonderful! You made five collections — and one of them is empty. An empty box is still a collection.
sort.successShape: Wonderful! Every item is in exactly one collection.

venn.title: Shade a set, discover its name
venn.subtitle: Click regions of the diagram (or use the buttons). The explorer names the set you have made and lists its elements.
venn.diagram: Venn diagram of A and B inside the universe U
venn.challenge: Challenge: two regions can be shaded in six different ways. Can you find all six, and name each one?

int.title: Walking the number line
int.subtitle: Adding a negative number walks to the left. Every integer has an opposite that walks you home to zero.
int.home: You came home to 0! The number you added is the opposite of where you started.
int.addHint: Can you find the number that brings you exactly home to 0?
int.twice: The opposite of the opposite is where you started: −(−a) = a.
int.flipHint: Taking the opposite reflects through zero. What happens if you do it twice?

arrow.title: Draw a function
arrow.subtitle: Click an element of A, then an element of B, to draw an arrow. Click the same pair again to remove it.
arrow.diagram: Arrow diagram from A to B
arrow.howTo: Click an element of A to start an arrow.
arrow.isFunction: Is it a function from A to B?
arrow.isFunctionYes: Yes: every element of A has exactly one arrow.
arrow.tooMany: {x} has more than one arrow — a function gives exactly one output.
arrow.noArrow: {x} has no arrow yet — a function needs an output for every input.
arrow.injectiveYes: No two arrows land on the same element.
arrow.surjectiveYes: Every element of B is hit.
arrow.bijectiveYes: A perfect pairing: you could reverse every arrow.
arrow.pigeonhole: With {m} inputs and only {n} outputs, two arrows must land together — so no function A → B can be injective. This is the pigeonhole principle.

comp.title: Composition machines
comp.subtitle: Feed a number through two machines. Does the order matter?
comp.sameEverywhere: Both orders agree for every input from −5 to 5. (Checking a range is evidence — can you prove they always agree?)
comp.sameHere: They agree for this input — but try others. Agreement at one input doesn’t mean the functions are equal.
comp.different: Different results: {a} versus {b}. The order of composition matters.
comp.goldIs: Gold dashed arrows show g ∘ f, which goes straight from A to C.
comp.chainNote: Change f or g and watch g ∘ f update. To compute (g ∘ f)(x), follow the arrow from x to B, then from there to C.

inv.title: The partner search
inv.subtitle: For each integer a, search for a partner b that brings you back to the identity.
inv.zero: Zero times anything is 0, never 1. Zero has no multiplicative partner in any number system.
inv.none: No integer works — and searching further wouldn’t help (can you see why?).
inv.fraction: Outside the integers there is a partner: b = {b}. Fractions fix the problem the integers can’t.
inv.onlyOnes: Among the integers, only 1 and −1 have multiplicative partners.

clock.title: The clock laboratory
clock.subtitle: On a clock with k hours, counting wraps around. Explore adding and multiplying.
clock.addNote: {sum} hours forward on a {k}-hour clock lands on {end}: the remainder when {sum} is divided by {k}.
clock.partners: Numbers with a multiplicative partner (a 1 in their row):
clock.pattern: These are exactly the numbers that share no common factor with k other than 1:

rem.title: Remainder families
rem.subtitle: Colour each integer by its remainder after dividing by k. Every integer lands in exactly one family.
rem.line: Integers from −15 to 15 coloured by remainder
rem.addTitle: Add a member of one family to a member of another…
rem.always: Every time, the sum lands in family [{r}]. The family of a sum depends only on the families — not on which members you picked.

boxes.title: Boxes inside boxes
boxes.subtitle: Start with one empty box. Build new collections by putting boxes into boxes.
boxes.wrap: Put it in a new box
boxes.together: Put them together in a box
boxes.howTo: Select one box to wrap, or several to put together.
boxes.already: You already have {set} — a collection is determined by what is inside, so this is the same box.
boxes.vonNeumann: Look at the boxes the magic wand builds: ∅ has 0 elements, {∅} has 1, {∅, {∅}} has 2… Each new box contains all the earlier ones. Some mathematicians use exactly these sets to define the counting numbers.

cat.title: Arrows that compose
cat.subtitle: Click arrows to build a path. Every path composes to a single arrow — and brackets never matter.
cat.cannot: Can’t compose: {last} ends at {end}, but {next} starts at {start}.
cat.brackets: Two ways to bracket h ∘ g ∘ f
cat.same: The last two columns always agree: h ∘ (g ∘ f) = (h ∘ g) ∘ f. That is associativity.

prod.title: The product, by its maps
prod.subtitle: Choose maps f : Z → A and g : Z → B. Then try to build a map h : Z → A × B that projects back to f and g.
prod.badFirst: First coordinates don’t match: h({z}) starts with {a}, but f({z}) = {fa}.
prod.badSecond: Second coordinates don’t match: h({z}) ends with {b}, but g({z}) = {gb}.
prod.challenge: Your turn: choose h(p), h(q), h(r) by clicking cells.
prod.unique: It works — and look: your h is exactly ⟨f, g⟩. There was only one possible choice. That uniqueness is what “universal” means.

diag.title: The diagonal machine
diag.subtitle: Here is a list of infinite 0–1 sequences (we can only show the start). The gold sequence d flips the diagonal.
diag.differs: d differs from s{i} in position {i}: s{i} has {a} there, d has {b}.
diag.hover: Point at (or tab to) a row to see where d differs from it. Click any digit to change the list.
diag.note: Add d to the list and a new d appears that is different again. No list — however long — can contain every sequence.
